opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was a pretty intense period. When FTX collapsed in late 2022, a lot of people and projects in AI safety had been counting on funding from the FTX Future Fund, and suddenly it wasn't there, sometimes with commitments only partly paid out. At Open Philanthropy we set up a process to look at those cases fairly quickly, and I ended up evaluating a lot of grants in a short window.

What it did for me, more than anything, was force me to look at a really broad cross-section of the technical safety field all at once. Normally you see proposals trickle in, you go deep on each one, and you have time to form a careful view. In the emergency setting I was looking at dozens of projects across interpretability, adversarial robustness, evals, theory, field-building, and having to make calls fast. That gave me a sense of the landscape I don't think I'd have gotten otherwise: where there was a lot of energy, where there were real gaps, and how much variance there was in how clearly people could explain the theory of change behind their work.

One big lesson was that the bottleneck was often less about money and more about legible, well-scoped research directions that a grantmaker could evaluate. A lot of people really wanted to work on safety but didn't have a crisp answer to "what experiment would you run, and what would you learn if it worked?" That pushed me toward thinking we should be more proactive: putting out clearer requests for proposals, describing the specific research agendas we were excited about, instead of mostly reacting to whatever came in the door.

It also made me more comfortable with a somewhat higher-variance, faster grantmaking style. When you're forced to decide quickly, you notice that a lot of the extra deliberation you'd normally do doesn't change the decision much. So I came away thinking that for a growing field, being responsive and getting money to promising people quickly is often worth more than squeezing out the last bit of certainty on each grant.

And honestly, it was a reminder of how fragile the funding ecosystem was. Having so much of the field depend on one or two sources is risky, and that's stayed on my mind when thinking about how to build something more robust.

r001.rationale: She says emergency decisions came quickly, contrasting them with the time normally available to investigate proposals deeply.

r002.rationale: She favors fundable research directions with a clear theory of change and concrete experiments and expected learnings, communicating a desire for more substantive justification.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so for context, when FTX collapsed in late 2022, the Future Fund had been a major funder of a lot of AI safety work, and overnight a bunch of people and organizations were in a really precarious spot. Some had received money they were now worried about clawbacks on, some had been promised money that just evaporated, and a lot of them were small teams with a few months of runway at best. So at Open Phil we had to move pretty fast to figure out who to backfill and who not to.

And I think the biggest thing that experience did for me was force a kind of clarity that normal grantmaking doesn't. In the ordinary course of things, you have time. You can ask for a longer proposal, you can wait for a research output to land, you can talk to five references. In that period, you basically had to make a call in days or weeks on whether a given project was something you actually believed in, with incomplete information, and knowing that a "no" might mean the thing just stops existing.

What that surfaced for me was how much of my prior grantmaking had been implicitly leaning on the fact that someone else was also funding the thing. There's this diffusion of responsibility where if a project has multiple funders, you can be sort of lukewarm on it and still contribute, because you're not the one deciding whether it lives or dies. When that cushion disappeared, I had to actually ask: if it were only me, would I fund this? And for a fair number of things, the honest answer was more uncertain than I had let myself believe. That was uncomfortable but useful.

The second thing it did was sharpen my sense of the difference between funding people versus funding agendas. In an emergency, you don't really have the luxury of evaluating a research direction in depth. You're mostly making a bet on whether this person or this team has good judgment and will do something reasonable with the money. And I came away thinking that in technical AI safety specifically, that's actually closer to the right frame most of the time anyway, because the field is so early and the agendas shift so quickly. The people who had a clear story about why their work mattered and what they'd do if it didn't pan out were much easier to say yes to than people who had an impressive-sounding agenda but couldn't articulate the theory of change.

And then the third thing, honestly, is that it made me more conservative about the structural side. I became a lot more attentive to how concentrated the funding base for a given organization was, and whether people were building plans around money that could disappear. Part of the job of a funder, I now think, is not just to pick good projects but to avoid creating a situation where the whole field is one bad quarter away from a crisis. So I pay more attention now to runway, to diversification, to whether we're inadvertently making people fragile by being too easy to rely on.

So I'd say the net effect was it made me more honest about my own convictions, more focused on judgment over proposals, and more cautious about the ecosystem-level fragility that a few big funders can create.

r001.rationale: Cotra says emergency decisions had to be made in days or weeks, with incomplete information and without time for lengthy proposals, research outputs, or multiple references.

r002.rationale: She describes asking whether she would fund a project on her own conviction and says she favored people who could explain why their work mattered and their theory of change over those with merely impressive-sounding agendas.

astra-6.text:
It made the importance of the funding ecosystem much more concrete for me. In an emergency, you’re asking which projects might otherwise fall apart, what you can assess quickly, and where continuity matters enough to justify acting with less certainty than you’d normally want.

That’s a different question from asking which projects you would fund if you were designing a portfolio from scratch. You don’t want a short-term funding shock to determine which research directions survive. But you also don’t want an emergency grant to become an implicit commitment to fund a project indefinitely.

The broader lesson for technical AI safety grantmaking is that you need both responsiveness and independent judgment. You want enough flexibility to preserve promising work through a disruption, while still coming back to the substantive question: how would this research actually help us make advanced AI safer?

r001.rationale: The response says emergency grants required deciding what could be assessed quickly and acting with less certainty, conveying that urgency constrained how deeply grants could be assessed.

r002.rationale: It calls for independent judgment and asks how research would help make AI safer, but does not clearly state that Cotra wanted grantmaking to rely more on inside-view justification for the research directions funded.

sol-6.1.text:
That experience made me think harder about the distinction between evaluating a research proposal and evaluating whether someone is well positioned to do useful research. In an emergency, you’re often looking at people whose funding disappeared unexpectedly, and the immediate question is: should they be able to keep working while we figure out the longer-term picture?

I think there’s a case for giving researchers enough stability and flexibility to pursue ideas that might not fit neatly into a proposal. In technical AI safety, we’re uncertain about which approaches will work, and the research can change direction pretty quickly. You don’t want every change of direction to require a whole new grant application.

But that doesn’t remove the need for judgment. You still need to ask what you’ve learned from the work, whether the person is responding to evidence, and whether continuing makes sense. So the balance I’d want is room to explore, with substantive conversations about progress, rather than treating completion of the original plan as the main measure of success.

r001.rationale: The response mentions emergency grants and unexpected funding loss, but does not say the urgency limited Cotra’s ability to investigate individual grants deeply.

r002.rationale: The response supports flexibility and substantive conversations about progress, but does not clearly say grant decisions should use more inside-view justification for the research directions being funded.
